1    1.      Jurisdiction & Service

2            This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action under the Class Action Fairness

3    Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d), as this is a class action in which at least some members of the proposed

4    Class are citizens of a different State than Defendant and the claims of the proposed Class Members

5    exceed $5,000,000 in the aggregate.

6            Meazure was initially served with the complaint in the Perjanik and McDowell actions,

7    and was served with the consolidated amended complaint via ECF on June 23, 2025.

8    2.      Facts
9    Plaintiffs’ Statement: Plaintiffs brought this action against ProctorU, Inc. d/b/a Meazure Learning
10   (“Meazure”), seeking relief individually and behalf of all those whose Bar Examinations were
11   disrupted because of Meazure’s software malfunction.
12           For the February 2025 Exam, the State Bar contracted with Meazure for the remote
13   proctoring software that test-takers were required to use to complete the exam on a computer.
14   Applicants who do not wish to handwrite the exam are required to use Meazure’s Platform and to
15   pay a fee to Meazure to take the test. Meazure knew well in advance how many thousands of
16   applicants would be taking the Exam, as thousands sign up for the CA Bar Exam each February
17   and each July. Meazure also knew how important the CA Bar Exam is for test takers. It understands
18   that the expenses associated with the test are significant, and that failure to pass the bar will prevent

19   law graduates from working as attorneys within the state of California.

20           Plaintiffs and Class Members invested significant time and money to prepare for the Exam.

21   They spent hundreds of hours studying, they invested in expensive test-preparation classes, and

22   they paid hefty fees to both the State Bar and to Meazure to take the Exam using its Platform. They

23   also spent time and money traveling to testing locations and taking practice tests to familiarize

24   themselves with the Platform. Despite the tremendous stakes associated with the CA Bar Exam,

25   on February 25 and 26, 2025, Meazure’s testing software crashed repeatedly during the Exam.

26   Meazure’s testing software crashed because it had insufficient infrastructure and/or lack of servers

1    and server space to process the foreseeable number of exam takers. Meazure failed to design,

2    maintain, and/or improve the infrastructure of the exam software to sufficiently and adequately

3    service Plaintiffs and Class Members who had no choice but to pay Meazure’s fee to take the Exam

4    on a computer.

5            As a result of Meazure’s failure to have a properly functioning software available for

6    applicants, Plaintiffs and the Class did not receive what they paid for – working test software that

7    would let them complete one of the most important tests of their careers. Plaintiffs sat for the CA

8    Bar Exam and suffered injury from these technical failures. Plaintiffs seek monetary redress and
9    injunctive relief for themselves and the proposed Class who were injured when the February 2025
10   CA Bar Exam fell apart due to Meazure’s failures.
11           Defendant’s Statement: Meazure Learning contracted with the State Bar to administer

15   Learning denies that it caused any Plaintiff any injury. Meazure Learning does not adopt or agree

12          Plaintiffs’ position is that unitary, not bifurcated, discovery is appropriate. The issues

13   related to Plaintiffs’ individual claims and the class certification issues, on the one hand, and class

14   merits discovery, on the other, substantially overlap. See Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S.

15   338, 351 (2011) (“Frequently [the class certification] ‘rigorous analysis’ will entail some overlap

16   with the merits of the plaintiff’s underlying claim. That cannot be helped. The class determination

17   generally involves considerations that are enmeshed in the factual and legal issues comprising the

18   plaintiff’s cause of action.”). For example, if, as Plaintiffs allege, Meazure breached its warranties

19   as to its Platform, they breached them as to all class members. Similarly, whether and the extent

20   to which Meazure’s Platform malfunctioned is a common question of fact as to all class members.

21   And Meazure’s defenses, including its position that Plaintiffs did not pay Meazure directly, are

22   also common to the class.

23          Attempting to untangle which discrete categories of discovery can be deferred until some

24   later portion of the case because they are relevant only to class merits and not to individual merits

25   or a rigorous analysis of the Rule 23 factors is likely to generate more discovery disputes, not

14

 1          In sum, because Plaintiffs cannot plead an actionable misrepresentation or omission, and

 3
     CLRA, FAL, and UCL (Claims 4, 5, and 8) all fail and must be dismissed.
 4

 5   III.   Plaintiffs’ Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress Claim (Claim 6) Fails.

 6          In California, “there is no independent tort of negligent infliction of emotional distress.”

 7   Potter v. Firestone Tire & Rubber Co., 863 P.2d 795, 807 (Cal. 1993). Rather, “[t]he tort is
 8   negligence, a cause of action in which a duty to the plaintiff is an essential element.” Id. In
 9
     negligence cases alleging emotional distress, “unless the defendant has assumed a duty to plaintiff
10
     in which the emotional condition of the plaintiff is an object, recovery is available only if the
11
     emotional distress arises out of the defendant’s breach of some other legal duty and the emotional
12

13   distress is proximately caused by that breach of duty.” Id. at 807–08.

14          Plaintiffs’ negligent infliction of emotional distress (“NIED”) claim must be dismissed

15   pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) because Meazure owed no duty to Plaintiffs, and the emotional distress
16
     that Plaintiffs allege does not support a claim for NIED.
17
            A.      Meazure Did Not Owe a Legal Duty to Plaintiffs to Protect Their Emotional
18                  Well-Being.
19
            In support of their NIED claim, Plaintiffs only allege that Meazure “had a duty to provide
20
     a platform free of defects that would allow users to take and complete the exam.” (Compl. ¶ 200.)
21
     Duty for negligence purposes may (1) be imposed by law, (2) be assumed by the defendant, or
22
     (3) exist by virtue of a special relationship. Friedman v. Merck & Co., 131 Cal. Rptr. 2d 885, 890
23

24   (Ct. App. 2003). Plaintiffs, however, have not sufficiently alleged that Meazure owes a duty under

25   any of these circumstances to protect their emotional well-being.
26          First, Plaintiffs have not identified any duty imposed on Meazure to protect users of its
27
     software from the emotional distress of a technical failure.
28

 3
     the center of the service. See Friedman, 131 Cal. Rptr. 2d at 898–99. Examples include services
 4
     such as a therapist who agrees to treat a patient, or a mortuary’s duty to the family of the deceased.
 5
     Id. There was no duty assumed by Meazure in these circumstances.

 7          Finally, Meazure was not in a special relationship with Plaintiffs. “Typically, in special

 8   relationships, the plaintiff is particularly vulnerable and dependent upon the defendant who,

 9   correspondingly, has some control over the plaintiff’s welfare.” Carlsen v. Koivumaki, 174 Cal.
10
     Rptr. 3d 339, 353 (Ct. App. 2014). A defendant who “is found to have a ‘special relationship’ with
11
     another may owe an affirmative duty to protect the other person from foreseeable harm, or to come
12
     to the aid of another in the face of ongoing harm or medical emergency.” Id. No such relationship
13
     exists here. See Runner v. C.R. Bard, 108 F. Supp. 3d 261, 272 (E.D. Pa. 2015) (no special
14

15   relationship between consumer and prescription surgical mesh medical product manufacturer that

16   would create an “implied duty to care for the plaintiff’s emotional wellbeing”). Plaintiffs have not
17   alleged any special relationship between a software developer or a test taker that would create a
18

20                  Distress Damages.

22

23

24

25   simply damage to property or financial interests.” Potter, 863 P.2d at 808.
